title: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
hookLine: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead; "the beginning of the good news"

cards: So many of those words lead back to four short books: the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. On day seven you heard that a lot of people start reading the Bible with a Gospel.
The shortest of the four is Mark. Sixteen chapters. You could read the whole thing aloud in one sitting, in somebody's living room.
It's fast. It's blunt. It skips the parts you'd expect.
There's no Christmas in it, no shepherds, no star. It starts with a man shouting in the desert. And its very first line is today's word.

teach.b: Mark, chapter one, verse one. In the old English: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole verse.
It's a title, and a door. Start with gospel: good news. Mark's Greek word is euangelion, and it wasn't a church word yet.
Historians point to Roman-era inscriptions that use it for public announcements: a victory won, news about an emperor, news that changes the day for everyone who hears it.
Mark takes that word and puts it on a builder from Galilee. Now the shape, so you know the mountain ahead.

teach.h: THE TURN: WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?
teach.b: First, Galilee: a man baptized in a river, fishermen dropping their nets, healings, arguments, and the stories he told. A word Mark uses again and again here is straightway. Immediately.
Everything happens fast. Then, right in the middle, the turning point. Jesus asks his friends: who do you say that I am?
And from there the road turns toward Jerusalem.

The last third of the book is one week: the entry into the city, the table and the bread, the cross, and the empty tomb, where the women run away, afraid. Which brings us back to the book's first word. Beginning.
Some readers notice that Mark calls all of it, the whole book, just the beginning.

teach.h: THE BEGINNING OF THE GOOD NEWS.
teach.b: As if the good news isn't finished when the book ends. As if the reader is supposed to pick it up from there.

how: Christians hear the Gospels read aloud in church, and some churches follow a cycle of readings in which one year draws largely on Mark. Some groups read the whole of Mark aloud in one sitting.

s: Mark's Gospel opens with the Christmas story
Mark has no birth story at all. it opens with a man shouting in the desert.
Mark is the shortest of the four Gospels
sixteen chapters. you can read it aloud in one sitting.
euangelion was a church word before the Christians used it
outside the church it was used for good news announced in public, like a victory.

games.q: you're writing a Gospel. everyone wants to know about this man. where do you begin?
o: with his birth in Bethlehem and a star.
with the beginning of the world.
with a man shouting in the desert, and a title: the beginning of the gospel.
games.why: Mark skips the birth entirely. "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ" — and then straight into the desert. fast, blunt, no Christmas.

practice: Last sit of the camp. Sit, and breathe, the way you did on day one, when the first word was communion, a meal that remembers. Now let one word from these three weeks come back to you on its own.
Don't pick it. Let it arrive. Grace, maybe.
Or the stone already moved. Or small is enough. Hold it for a few breaths.
Then ask, gently: where does this start for me? If you pray, you can offer that word back as your prayer, with an amen. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be a beginning.

wordCard.voice: Mark 1:1. The beginning of the gospel: good news, and only the beginning of it. Twenty-first word, and the strand is complete.

orig.note: Greek, Mark 1:1: the beginning of the good news. the first words of the shortest Gospel.
